entities.name: Hohenschwangau Castle
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
Hohenschwangau Castle, constructed between 1832 and 1837, is a striking example of 19th-century Romantic architecture located in Bavaria, Germany. Commissioned by King Maximilian II of Bavaria, the castle embodies the revival of medieval styles and serves as a precursor to the more famous Neuschwanstein Castle, which was built nearby. The castle's significance lies in its reflection of the cultural and political currents of the time, particularly the Bavarian nationalism and the fascination with the medieval past that characterized the Romantic movement in Europe.

The construction of Hohenschwangau Castle was a family project for the Bavarian royal house, designed by architect Georg Friedrich von Gärtner, and it was built on the site of a former castle that had fallen into ruins. The interiors are lavishly decorated with frescoes that depict heroic legends and romanticized views of nature, showcasing the artistic trends of the era. The castle served not only as a royal residence but also as a retreat for the young Ludwig II, who would later ascend the throne and become known for his extravagant building projects, including the iconic Neuschwanstein.

Hohenschwangau's legacy includes influencing the architectural landscape of Bavaria and shaping the cultural identity of the region. The castle attracts millions of tourists each year, contributing significantly to the local economy and becoming emblematic of the Bavarian Alps' romantic allure. The preservation efforts surrounding the castle also reflect broader trends in heritage conservation that emerged in the 20th century, as societies sought to maintain and celebrate their historical environments.
